arXiv:1911.02157v1 [math.AP] 06 Nov 2019

Global weak solutions and asymptotics of a singular PDE-ODE chemotaxis system with discontinuous data

Hongyun Peng Address: School of Applied Mathematics, Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, 510006, China Email address: hypengmath@gdut.edu.cn , Zhi-An Wang Address: Department of Applied Mathematics, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hung Hom, Kowloon, Hong Kong Email address: mawza@polyu.edu.hk and Changjiang Zhu Address: School of Mathematics, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, 510641, China Email address: machjzhu@scut.edu.cn
Abstract.

This paper is concerned with the well-posedness and large-time behavior of a two dimensional PDE-ODE hybrid chemotaxis system describing the initiation of tumor angiogenesis. We first transform the system via a Cole-Hopf type transformation into a parabolic-hyperbolic system and show that the solution of the transformed system converges to a constant equilibrium state as time tends to infinity. Finally we reverse the Cole-Hopf transformation and obtain the relevant results for the pre-transformed PDE-ODE hybrid system. In contrast to the existing related results, where continuous initial datum is imposed, we are able to prove the asymptotic stability for discontinuous initial data with large oscillations. The key ingredient in our proof is the use of so-called “effective viscous flux”, which enables us to obtain the desired energy estimates and regularity. The technique of “effective viscous flux” turns out to be a very useful tool to study chemotaxis systems with initial data having low regularity and was rarely (if not) used in the literature for chemotaxis models.

Key words and phrases: 
Chemotaxis, asymptotic stability, discontinuous initial data, effective viscous flux
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
35A01, 35B40, 35Q92, 92C17

1. Introduction

In this paper we consider the following PDE-ODE hybrid chemotaxis model

{ut=Δu−∇⋅(ξu∇lnc),ct=−μ​u​c\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(\xi u\nabla\ln c),\\ c_{t}=-\mu uc\end{array}\right.

which was proposed in [28] to describe the interaction between signaling molecules vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and vascular endothelial cells during the initiation of tumor angiogenesis (see also in [5, 6]), where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and c⁡(x,t)c(x,t) denote the density of vascular endothelial cells and concentration of VEGF, respectively. The parameter ξ>0\xi>0 is referred to as the chemotactic coefficient measuring the strength of chemotaxis and μ\mu denotes the degradation rate of the chemical VEGF. Here the chemical diffusion is neglected since it is far less important than its interaction with endothelial cells (cf. [28]). On the other hand, the system (1) can also be regarded as a particular form of the well-known Keller-Segel system proposed in the seminal paper [25] describing the propagation of traveling wave band formed by bacterial chemotaxis observed in the experiment of Adler [2].

The distinguishing feature of the model (1) is twofold: (i) the first equation of (1) contains a logarithmic sensitivity function ln⁡c\ln c which is singular at c=0{c=0} but is a very meaningful sensitivity representation (cf. [40, 24]; (ii) the second equation of (1) is an ODE and hence lacks a spatial structure. Either of these features is the source of challenges for mathematical analysis and numerical computations. To overcome these obstacles, a Cole-Hopf type transformation

𝐯=−1μ∇(lnc)=−1μ∇cc{\bf v}=-\frac{1}{\mu}\nabla(\ln c)=-\frac{1}{\mu}\frac{\nabla c}{c} (1.4)

has been introduced in [27, 45], which transforms the system (1) into a parabolic-hyperbolic system:

{ut−χ∇⋅(u𝐯)=Δu,𝐯t−∇u=0,\begin{cases}u_{t}-\chi\nabla\cdot(u{\bf v})=\Delta u,\\ {\bf v}_{t}-\nabla u=0,\end{cases} (1.5)

where χ=μ​ξ>0\chi=\mu\xi>0, 𝐯{\bf v} is a gradient vector and curl𝐯=0{\bf v}=0. Apparently the transformed system (1.5) is much more manipulable mathematically than the original system (1) since the singularity vanishes and the quantity 𝐯{\bf v} possesses a spatial structure through uu. In this paper, we shall consider the well-posedness and asymptotic behavior of solutions to (1.5) with initial data

(u,𝐯)​(x,0)=(u0,𝐯0)​(x),x∈ℝ2(u,{\bf v})(x,0)=(u_{0},{\bf v}_{0})(x),\ \ x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} (1.6)

subject to the following asymptotic states

(u,𝐯)​(±∞,t)=(u¯,𝟎),(u,{\bf v})(\pm\infty,t)=(\bar{u},{\bf 0}), (1.7)

where (u¯,𝟎)(\bar{u},{\bf 0}) with u¯>0\bar{u}>0 is a constant ground state of (1.5)). Then we reverse the Cole-Hopf transformation (1.4) and get the well-posedness and asymptotic behavior of solutions to the original PDE-ODE chemotaxis system (1).

There has been a considerable amount of interesting works carried out for the transformed system (1.5). The one-dimensional problem has been first studied extensively from various aspects such as the traveling wave solutions [22, 34, 35, 32, 39, 41, 44], global dynamics of solutions in the whole space [12, 30, 49, 37] or in the bounded interval [19, 31, 33, 48]. For the multidimensional whole space ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, the nonlinear stability of planar traveling wave was recently established in [3]. When the initial datum is close to the constant ground state (u¯,𝟎)(\bar{u},{\bf 0}), numerous results have been obtained to the system (1.5). First the blowup criteria of classical solutions was established in [8, 29] and the long-time behavior of solutions was obtained in [29] if (u0−u¯,𝐯𝟎)∈Hs​(ℝd)(u_{0}-\bar{u},{\bf v_{0}})\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for s>d2+1s>\frac{d}{2}+1 and ∥(u0−u¯,𝐯𝟎)∥Hs×Hs\lVert(u_{0}-\bar{u},{\bf v_{0}})\rVert_{H^{s}\times H^{s}} is small. Later, Hao [13] established the global existence of mild solutions in the critical Besov space B˙2,1−12×(B˙2,112)d\dot{B}_{2,1}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(\dot{B}_{2,1}^{\frac{1}{2}})^{d} with minimal regularity in the Chemin-Lerner space framework. The global well-posedness of strong solutions of (1.5) in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} was established in [7] if ∥(u0−u¯,𝐯𝟎)∥L2×H1\lVert(u_{0}-\bar{u},{\bf v_{0}})\rVert_{L^{2}\times H^{1}} is small. If the initial datum has a higher regularity such that ∥(u0−u¯,𝐯𝟎)∥H2×H1\lVert(u_{0}-\bar{u},{\bf v_{0}})\rVert_{H^{2}\times H^{1}} is small, the algebraic decay of solutions was further derived in [7]. Wang, Xiang and Yu [47] established the global existence and time decay rates of solutions of (1.5) in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d=2,3d=2,3 if (u0−u¯,𝐯𝟎)∈H2​(ℝd)(u_{0}-\bar{u},{\bf v_{0}})\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and ∥(u0−u¯,𝐯𝟎)∥H1×H1\lVert(u_{0}-\bar{u},{\bf v_{0}})\rVert_{H^{1}\times H^{1}} is small. Recently the small energy solution in ℝd​(d=2,3)\mathbb{R}^{d}(d=2,3) was established in [46]. In the multidimensional bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd​(d=2,3)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}(d=2,3), the global existence and exponential decay rates of solutions under Neumann boundary conditions were obtained in [33, 42] for small data, and local existence of classical solutions in two dimensions with Dirichlet boundary conditions was given in [20]. When the Laplacian (diffusion) in (1.5) was modified to a fractional Laplacian, the global existence of solutions of (1.5) in a torus with periodic boundary conditions in some dissipation regimes was established in [10, 11].

In the above-mentioned results, all solutions obtained for (1.5) are classical thanks to the high regularity and smallness of the Hs​(s≥1)H^{s}(s\geq 1)-norm on the initial data. The goal of this paper is to exploit the parabolic-hyperbolic system (1.5) with rougher initial data which are allowed to be discontinuous and possess large amplitude. Specifically we consider the initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) in some appropriate LpL^{p} space and allow ∥u0−u¯∥L∞+∥𝐯0∥L∞\lVert u_{0}-\bar{u}\rVert_{L^{\infty}}+\lVert\mathbf{v}_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}} to be arbitrarily large. The low regularity of initial data and large amplitude bring us many new difficulties in analysis compared to the existing works (cf. [7, 29, 47]). In particular, the integrability of ∇𝐯\nabla{\bf v}, which plays a crucial role in the analysis of [7, 29, 47], can be easily attained therein but appears to be unattainable for our less regular initial data due to the hyperbolic effect of the second equation. Hence one can only expect to examine LpL^{p}-integrability for 𝐯{\bf v} and hence obtain weak solutions instead of strong (classical) solutions. The key idea of gaining LpL^{p}-integrability of 𝐯{\bf v} developed in this paper is to rewrite the first equation of (1.5) as u~t=∇⋅𝐅\tilde{u}_{t}=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} inspired by the works [15, 36] on the Navier-Stokes equations, where 𝐅\mathbf{F} is the so called “effective viscous flux” defined by

𝐅=∇u+χ​u​𝐯.\mathbf{F}=\nabla u+\chi u\bf{v}. (1.8)

Then we rewrite the second equation of (1.5) as

𝐯t=−χ​u​𝐯+𝐅{\bf v}_{t}=-\chi u{\bf v}+{\bf F}

and try to attain the regularity of 𝐯{\bf v} through 𝐅{\bf F} whose regularity is easier than 𝐯{\bf v} to obtain. We remark that the dynamics of PDEs with discontinuous data has been an important topic arising from fluid mechanics and gas dynamics in order to understand how the discontinuity evolves in the fluid. For this, Hoff with his collaborators have developed some nice ideas and obtained a series of important results in this aspect (cf. [14, 15, 16, 17, 18]). We refer to [4, 21, 26, 38] and references therein for further development on the discontinuous data problem. However in our current work the “effective viscous flux” 𝐅{\bf F} exists in its divergence form (i.e. OPEN∇⋅𝐅)\nabla\cdot{\bf F}), which is different from that used in the Navier-Stokes equations where the “effective viscous flux” exists in its gradient form and LpL^{p}-norm of ∇𝐅\nabla{\bf F} can be achieved directly (cf. [15, 16, 17, 18, 36]). This implies that besides the estimate of ∇⋅𝐅\nabla\cdot{\bf F}, we have to estimate for the curl of 𝐅{\bf F} (denoted by ∇⊥𝐅\nabla^{\bot}{\bf F}) in order to get the estimates for ∇𝐅\nabla{\bf F} and hence the regularity for 𝐅{\bf F}, which is a key difference from the Navier-Stokes equation. The “effective viscous flux” technique appears to be a very powerful tool to study chemotaxis systems with low regular initial data and was rarely (if not) used in the literature.

Since the dependence of solutions on χ\chi and u¯\bar{u} is not the interest of this paper, we henceforth assume χ=u¯=1\chi=\bar{u}=1 throughout the paper for simplicity without further clarification.

To state our results, we first introduce the definition of weak solutions of (1.5)-(1.7).

Definition 1.1 (Weak solutions).

We say that (u,𝐯)(u,{\bf v}) is a weak solution of (1.5)-(1.7), if (u,𝐯)(u,{\bf v}) is suitably integrable and satisfies for all test functions Ψ∈C0∞​(ℝ2×[0,∞))\Psi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\times[0,\infty)) that

∫ℝ2u0​Ψ0​𝑑x+∫0∞∫ℝ2(u​Ψt−∇u⋅∇Ψ)​𝑑x​𝑑t=∫0∞∫ℝ2u​𝐯⋅∇Ψ​𝑑x​𝑑t\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u_{0}\Psi_{0}dx+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(u\Psi_{t}-\nabla u\cdot\nabla\Psi\right)dxdt=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u{\bf v}\cdot\nabla\Psi dxdt\end{split}

and

∫ℝ2𝐯0j​Ψ0​dx+∫0∞∫ℝ2(𝐯j​Ψt−u​Ψxj)​dx​dt=0,\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}{\bf v}_{0}^{j}\Psi_{0}dx+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left({\bf v}^{j}\Psi_{t}-u\Psi_{x_{j}}\right)dxdt=0,\end{split}

where j=1,2j=1,2 and Ψ0​(x)=Ψ⁡(x,0)\Psi_{0}(x)=\Psi(x,0).

Then our main results in this paper are given as follows:

Theorem 1.1.

Let 4<p0<∞4<p_{0}<\infty and the initial data satisfy

u0−1∈L2​(ℝ2),𝐯0∈L2​(ℝ2)∩Lp0​(ℝ2),u0≥0,∇⊥⋅𝐯0=0u_{0}-1\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\ \ {\bf v}_{0}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\ \ u_{0}\geq 0,\ \ \nabla^{\bot}\cdot{\bf v}_{0}=0 (1.9)

where ∇⊥=(∂2,−∂1)\nabla^{\bot}=(\partial_{2},-\partial_{1}) denotes the curl operator. Then for any constant M>0M>0 with ‖𝐯0‖Lp0​(ℝ2)≤M\|{\bf v}_{0}\|_{L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq M, there exists a constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 depending on MM, such that if

∥u0−1∥L2​(ℝ2)2+∥𝐯𝟎∥L2​(ℝ2)2=θ0≤ε,\lVert u_{0}-1\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}+\lVert\mathbf{v_{0}}\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}=\theta_{0}\leq\varepsilon,

then the Cauchy problem (1.5)-(1.7) has a global weak solution (u,𝐯)​(x,t)(u,{\bf v})(x,t) satisfying

{u−1∈L∞([0,∞);L2(ℝ2))∩C((0,∞);C(ℝ2)),∇u∈L2([0,∞);L2(ℝ2)),𝐯∈L∞​([0,∞),L2​(ℝ2)∩Lp0​(ℝ2))∩C⁡([0,∞),H−1​(ℝ2)).\begin{cases}\begin{split}&u-1\in L^{\infty}([0,\infty);L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\cap C((0,\infty);C(\mathbb{R}^{2})),\ \nabla u\in L^{2}([0,\infty);L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})),\\ &{\bf v}\in L^{\infty}([0,\infty);L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\cap C([0,\infty),H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})).\end{split}\end{cases} (1.10)

and the following asymptotic convergence

∥u(x,t)−1∥Lp1​(ℝ2)→0,∥𝐯(x,t)∥Lp2​(ℝ2)→0ast→∞,\begin{split}\|u(x,t)-1\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0,\ \ \|{\bf v}(x,t)\|_{L^{p_{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0~~as~~t\to\infty,\end{split} (1.11)

where 2<p1≤∞2<p_{1}\leq\infty and 2<p2<p0<∞2<p_{2}<p_{0}<\infty.

Remark 1.1.

The above results hold true regardless of the strength of initial perturbation from the constant ground state (1,0)(1,0), namely the amplitude ∥u0−1∥L∞+∥𝐯𝟎∥𝐋∞\lVert u_{0}-1\rVert_{L^{\infty}}+\lVert\bf{v}_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}} can be arbitrarily large. The initial conditions (1.9) imply that the initial data of the Cauchy problem (1.5)-(1.7) could be discontinuous (such as piecewise constant with arbitrarily large jump discontinuities), which brings great challenges to the analysis. Moreover the condition ∇⊥⋅𝐯0=0\nabla^{\bot}\cdot{\bf v}_{0}=0 is a natural consequence the Cole-Hopf transformation (1.4).

To prove Theorem 1.1, we first mollify the initial data with a mollifying parameter δ\delta and obtain the global smooth solution (uδ,𝐯δ)(u^{\delta},\bf{v}^{\delta}) depending on the mollifying parameter δ\delta. Then we pass to the limit as δ→0\delta\to 0 and obtain a weak solution of (1.5)-(1.7). The core of the proof is to derive the global a priori estimates independent of the mollifying parameter δ\delta. In this connection, the approaches and estimates developed in previous works [29, 47] for small-amplitude and continuous initial data are not adequate for our current problem. In this paper, we shall introduce the so called “effective viscous flux” technique and make a full use of the structure of (1.5) to obtain the desired uniform-in-δ\delta estimates.

Converting the results from vv to cc by reversing the Cole-Hopf transformation (1.4), we get the results for the original chemotaxis model (1).

Theorem 1.2.

Let 4<p0<∞4<p_{0}<\infty and the initial data satisfy

u0−1∈L2​(ℝ2),u0​(x)≥0,∇ln⁡c0∈L2​(ℝ2)∩Lp0​(ℝ2)u_{0}-1\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\ \ u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ \nabla\ln c_{0}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})

Then for any constant M>0M>0 with ‖∇ln⁡c0‖Lp0​(ℝ2)≤M\|\nabla\ln c_{0}\|_{L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq M, there exists a constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 depending on MM, such that if

∥u0−1∥L2​(ℝ2)2+∥∇ln⁡c0∥L2​(ℝ2)2≤ε,\lVert u_{0}-1\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}+\lVert\nabla\ln c_{0}\rVert_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}\leq\varepsilon,

the Cauchy problem (1.5)-(1.7) has a global weak solution (u,c)​(x,t)(u,c)(x,t) satisfying

{u−1∈L∞([0,∞);L2(ℝ2)),∇u∈L2([0,∞);L2(ℝ2)),u−1∈C((0,∞);C(ℝ2)),∇lnc∈C([0,∞),H−1(ℝ2)),∇ln⁡c∈L∞​([0,∞),L2​(ℝ2)∩Lp0​(ℝ2))∩L4​([0,∞),L4​(ℝ2))\begin{cases}\begin{split}u-1&\in L^{\infty}([0,\infty);L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})),\ \ \ \ \nabla u\in L^{2}([0,\infty);L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})),\\ u-1&\in C((0,\infty);C(\mathbb{R}^{2})),\ \ \ {\nabla\ln c}\in C([0,\infty),H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})),\\ {\nabla\ln c}&\in L^{\infty}([0,\infty);L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cap L^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\cap L^{4}([0,\infty);L^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))\end{split}\end{cases}

and

∥u−1∥Lp1​(ℝ2)→0,∥∇lnc∥Lp2​(ℝ2)→0ast→∞,\begin{split}\|u-1\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0,\ \ \|\nabla\ln c\|_{L^{p_{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\to 0~~as~~t\to\infty,\end{split}

where 2<p1≤∞2<p_{1}\leq\infty and 2<p2<p0<∞2<p_{2}<p_{0}<\infty.

Furthermore, if c0∈L∞​(ℝ2),c0>0c_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\ c_{0}>0, then there exists a positive constant CC independent of tt such that the solution has the following decay rates in time:

∥c∥L∞​(ℝ2)≤C​e−34​t.\begin{split}\lVert c\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq Ce^{-\frac{3}{4}t}.\end{split} (1.12)

The rest of paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we collect some elementary facts and inequalities that will be used in later analysis. Section 3 is devoted to deriving the a priori estimates on smooth solutions. Then we prove Theorem 1.1 in Section 4. Finally we prove Theorem 1.2 in section 5.

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we will recall and prove some basic results that will be used later. Before embarking on this, we first introduce some notations used throughout this paper.

Notations.

  • •

    In what follows, CC denotes a generic positive constant which may vary in the context;

  • •

    Hk​(ℝ2)H^{k}(\mathbb{{R}}^{2}) denotes the usual kk-th order Sobolev space on ℝ2\mathbb{{R}}^{2} with norm

    ‖f‖Hk​(ℝ2):=(∑j=0k∫ℝ2|∂xjf|2​𝑑x)1/2.\|f\|_{H^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}:=\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{k}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|\partial_{x}^{j}f|^{2}dx\Big)^{1/2}.

    For simplicity, we denote ∥⋅∥:=∥⋅∥L2​(ℝ2)\|\cdot\|:=\|\cdot\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}, ∥⋅∥k:=∥⋅∥Hk​(ℝ2)\|\cdot\|_{k}:=\|\cdot\|_{H^{k}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}, and furthermore L2​(ℝ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) will be abbreviated as L2L^{2} without confusion.

  • •

    We denote the curl operator as

    ∇⊥=(∂2,−∂1),\nabla^{\bot}=(\partial_{2},-\partial_{1}), (2.1)
  • •

    For simplicity we set

    θ0=∥u0−1∥2+∥𝐯𝟎∥𝟐.\theta_{0}=\lVert u_{0}-1\rVert^{2}+\lVert\bf{v}_{0}\rVert^{2}. (2.2)

    Since θ0\theta_{0} will be assumed to be small in this paper, we assume that θ0<1\theta_{0}<1 without loss of generality in the sequel.

We start with the local existence and blowup criterion of smooth solutions to the Cauchy problem (1.5)-(1.7) established in [29, 8].

Lemma 2.1 ([29]).

Let s>d2+1s>\frac{d}{2}+1 and (u0−1,𝐯𝟎)∈Hs​(ℝd)(u_{0}-1,{\bf v_{0}})\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Then there exists a small-time T∗=T∗​(‖u0−1‖Hs,‖𝐯𝟎‖Hs​(ℝd))>0T_{*}=T_{*}(\|u_{0}-1\|_{H^{s}},\|{\bf v_{0}}\|_{H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{d})})>0 such that the Cauchy problem (1.5)-(1.7) a unique solution (u−1,𝐯)∈L∞​((0,T∗],Hs​(ℝd))(u-1,{\bf v})\in L^{\infty}((0,T_{*}],H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{d})).

Lemma 2.2 ([8]).

Let s>d2+1s>\frac{d}{2}+1 and (u0−1,𝐯𝟎)∈Hs​(ℝd)(u_{0}-1,{\bf v_{0}})\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Let (u,𝐯)(u,{\bf v}) be the unique local solution in Lemma 2.1 with the maximal lifespan T∗>0T_{*}>0. If

∫0T∗∥𝐯∥Lq​(ℝd)2​qq−d<∞,withd<q≤∞,\begin{split}\int_{0}^{T_{*}}\lVert{\bf v}\rVert_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{\frac{2q}{q-d}}<\infty,\ with\ d<q\leq\infty,\end{split} (2.3)

then the solution can be extended beyond T∗>0T_{*}>0.

Next, we introduce a change of variable u~=u−1\tilde{u}=u-1. Thus, the problem (1.5)-(1.6) turns into

{u~t−Δ​u~=∇⋅(u~​𝐯)+∇⋅𝐯,𝐯t−∇u~=0,(u~,𝐯)​(x,0)=(u0−1,𝐯0)​(x).\begin{cases}\tilde{u}_{t}-\Delta\tilde{u}=\nabla\cdot(\tilde{u}{\bf v})+\nabla\cdot{\bf v},\\ {\bf v}_{t}-\nabla\tilde{u}=0,\\ (\tilde{u},{\bf v})(x,0)=(u_{0}-1,{\bf v}_{0})(x).\end{cases} (2.4)

Then the “effective viscous flux” 𝐅{\bf F} defined in (1.8) can be written as

𝐅=∇u~+(u~+1)​𝐯.{\bf F}=\nabla\tilde{u}+(\tilde{u}+1)\bf{v}. (2.5)

By the first equation of (2.4), it is easy to see that

∇⋅𝐅=u~t.\nabla\cdot{\bf F}=\tilde{u}_{t}. (2.6)

Then 𝐅{\bf F} has the following useful estimate.

Lemma 2.3.

Let (u~,𝐯)(\tilde{u},{\bf v}) be a smooth solution of (2.4). Then there exists a positive constant CC such that

∥∇𝐅∥Lp≤C⁡(∥u~t∥Lp+∥∇⊥u~⋅𝐯∥Lp),\begin{split}\lVert\nabla{\bf F}\rVert_{L^{p}}\leq&C(\lVert\tilde{u}_{t}\rVert_{L^{p}}+\lVert\nabla^{\bot}\tilde{u}\cdot{\bf v}\rVert_{L^{p}}),\end{split} (2.7)

where p>1p>1.

Proof.

First we recall the following inequality (cf. Lemma 2.4(1) in [23]):

∥∇𝐅∥Lp≤C⁡(∥∇⋅𝐅∥Lp+∥∇⊥⋅𝐅∥Lp).\begin{split}\lVert\nabla{\bf F}\rVert_{L^{p}}\leq&C\big(\lVert\nabla\cdot{\bf F}\rVert_{L^{p}}+\lVert\nabla^{\bot}\cdot{\bf F}\rVert_{L^{p}}\big).\end{split} (2.8)

It then follows from (2.1) and (2.5) that

∇⊥⋅𝐅=∇⊥⋅∇u~+∇⊥⋅(u~​𝐯)+∇⊥⋅𝐯=∇⊥⋅(u~​𝐯)+∇⊥⋅𝐯=(u~+1)​∇⊥⋅𝐯+∇⊥u~⋅𝐯,\begin{split}\nabla^{\bot}\cdot{\bf F}=&\nabla^{\bot}\cdot\nabla\tilde{u}+\nabla^{\bot}\cdot(\tilde{u}{\bf v})+\nabla^{\bot}\cdot{\bf v}\\ =&\nabla^{\bot}\cdot(\tilde{u}{\bf v})+\nabla^{\bot}\cdot{\bf v}\\ =&(\tilde{u}+1)\nabla^{\bot}\cdot{\bf v}+\nabla^{\bot}\tilde{u}\cdot{\bf v},\end{split} (2.9)

where in the second equality we have used the fact that ∇⊥⋅∇=0\nabla^{\bot}\cdot\nabla=0. 3. A Priori Estimates for Approximate Solutions

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.1, by constructing approximate solutions based upon the following mollified initial data:

u~δ0=jδ∗u~0,𝐯0δ=jδ∗𝐯0,\begin{split}\tilde{u}^{\delta}_{0}=j^{\delta}*\tilde{u}_{0},\ \ \ {\bf v}_{0}^{\delta}=j^{\delta}*{\bf v}_{0},\end{split}

where u~0=u0−1\tilde{u}_{0}=u_{0}-1 and jδj^{\delta} is the standard mollifying kernel of width δ\delta (e.g. see [1]). Then we consider the following approximate system

{u~tδ−Δ​u~δ=∇⋅(u~δ​𝐯δ)+∇⋅𝐯δ,𝐯tδ−∇u~δ=0,\begin{cases}\tilde{u}^{\delta}_{t}-\Delta\tilde{u}^{\delta}=\nabla\cdot(\tilde{u}^{\delta}{\bf v}^{\delta})+\nabla\cdot{\bf v}^{\delta},\\ {\bf v}^{\delta}_{t}-\nabla\tilde{u}^{\delta}=0,\end{cases} (3.1)

with smooth initial data (u~0δ,𝐯0δ)(\tilde{u}^{\delta}_{0},{\bf v}_{0}^{\delta}) which satisfies

(u~0δ,𝐯0δ)∈H3​(ℝ2)(\tilde{u}^{\delta}_{0},{\bf v}^{\delta}_{0})\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) (3.2)

and

∥u~0δ∥2+∥𝐯0δ∥2≤∥u~0∥2+∥𝐯0∥2=θ0.\lVert\tilde{u}^{\delta}_{0}\rVert^{2}+\lVert{\bf v}^{\delta}_{0}\rVert^{2}\leq\lVert\tilde{u}_{0}\rVert^{2}+\lVert{\bf v}_{0}\rVert^{2}=\theta_{0}. (3.3)

By Lemma 2.1, we can obtain the local existence of solutions to the approximate system (3.1) with initial data (u0δ,𝐯0δ)(u^{\delta}_{0},{\bf v}_{0}^{\delta}) satisfying (3.2)-(3.3). Next, we shall show in a sequence of lemmas that these approximate solutions satisfy some global a priori estimates, independent of the mollifying parameter δ\delta. These estimates will then be applied in Section 4 to obtain the solutions of Theorem 1.1 as the limits of these approximate solutions.

For the sake of simplicity, we still use (u~,𝐯)(\tilde{u},{\bf v}) to represent the approximate solution (u~δ,𝐯δ)(\tilde{u}^{\delta},{\bf v}^{\delta}) in this section. Let T>0T>0 be a fixed time and (u~,𝐯)(\tilde{u},{\bf v}) be the smooth solution to (3.1) on ℝ2×(0,T]\mathbb{R}^{2}\times(0,T]. We set σ=σ⁡(t)=min⁡{1,t}\sigma=\sigma(t)=\min\{1,t\} and define

{A1​(T)≜supt∈[0,T](∥u~∥2+∥𝐯∥2)+∫0T∥∇u~∥2​dt,A2​(T)≜supt∈[0,T](σ​∥∇u~∥2+σ2​∥u~t∥2+σ2​∥𝐯t∥2)+∫0T(σ​∥u~t∥2+σ2​∥∇u~t∥2)​dt,A3​(T)≜supt∈[0,T]‖𝐯‖L44+∫0T‖𝐯‖L44​dt.\begin{cases}\begin{split}&A_{1}(T)\triangleq\sup\limits_{t\in[0,T]}\left(\lVert\tilde{u}\rVert^{2}+\lVert{\bf v}\rVert^{2}\right)+\int_{0}^{T}\lVert\nabla\tilde{u}\rVert^{2}dt,\\ &A_{2}(T)\triangleq\sup\limits_{t\in[0,T]}\left(\sigma\lVert\nabla\tilde{u}\rVert^{2}+\sigma^{2}\lVert\tilde{u}_{t}\rVert^{2}+\sigma^{2}\lVert{\bf v}_{t}\rVert^{2}\right)+\int_{0}^{T}\left(\sigma\lVert\tilde{u}_{t}\rVert^{2}+\sigma^{2}\lVert\nabla\tilde{u}_{t}\rVert^{2}\right)dt,\\ &A_{3}(T)\triangleq\sup\limits_{t\in[0,T]}\|{\bf v}\|_{L^{4}}^{4}+\int_{0}^{T}\|{\bf v}\|_{L^{4}}^{4}dt.\end{split}\end{cases} (3.4)

Next, we shall employ the technique of a priori assumption to derive the a priori estimates for the smooth solutions of (3.1)-(3.3). That is, we first assume that the smooth solution (u~,𝐯)(\tilde{u},{\bf v}) satisfies for any t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]

A1(T)≤2θ0,A2(T)≤2θ012,A3(T)≤2θ0η0,supt∈[0,T]∥𝐯∥Lp0≤6M,\begin{split}A_{1}(T)\leq 2\theta_{0},\ \ A_{2}(T)\leq 2\theta_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}},\ \ A_{3}(T)\leq 2\theta_{0}^{\eta_{0}},\ \ \sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|{\bf v}\|_{L^{p_{0}}}\leq 6M,\end{split} (3.5)

where MM and θ0\theta_{0} are from Theorem 1.1, and η0\eta_{0} is defined as

Then we will derive the a priori estimates to obtain global solutions. Finally, we show the obtained global solutions satisfy the above a priori assumption and close our argument.

Furthermore we have from (2.10) and (2.5) that

Thus, by (3.5) and (3.18), we have

where we have used the assumption θ0<1\theta_{0}<1 and the fact η0>0\eta_{0}>0.

By (2.7) and Hölder inequality, we have

∥u−1∥L∞→0​as​t→∞.\lVert u-1\rVert_{L^{\infty}}\to 0~~\text{as}~~t\to\infty. (4.9)

By the interpolation inequality, (4.7) and (4.9), for any 2<p1≤∞2<p_{1}\leq\infty, we have

∥u−1∥Lp1→0​as​t→∞.\lVert u-1\rVert_{L^{p_{1}}}\to 0~~\text{as}~~t\to\infty.

On the other hand, by (3.39), we have from (3.46) and (3.47) that

∫1∞|(∥𝐯∥L44)t|​dt≤C​∫1∞∫ℝ2|u~+1​|𝐯4​𝑑x​𝑑t+C​∫1∞∫ℝ2|𝐅||​𝐯|3​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C​∫1∞∫ℝ2𝐯4​𝑑x​𝑑t+C​∫1∞∫ℝ2|𝐅|​|𝐯|3​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C​∫1∞∫ℝ2𝐯4​𝑑x​𝑑t+C​∫1∞∫ℝ2|𝐅|4​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C.\begin{split}\int_{1}^{\infty}\left|\left(\lVert{\bf v}\rVert_{L^{4}}^{4}\right)_{t}\right|dt\leq&C\int_{1}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|\tilde{u}+1|{\bf v}^{4}dxdt+C\int_{1}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|{\bf F}||{\bf v}|^{3}dxdt\\ \leq&C\int_{1}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}{\bf v}^{4}dxdt+C\int_{1}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|{\bf F}||{\bf v}|^{3}dxdt\\ \leq&C\int_{1}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}{\bf v}^{4}dxdt+C\int_{1}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|{\bf F}|^{4}dxdt\\ \leq&C.\end{split}

Combining the above inequality with (3.47), we have

∥𝐯∥L4→0​as​t→∞,\lVert{\bf v}\rVert_{L^{4}}\to 0~~\text{as}~~t\to\infty,

which together with the interpolation inequality, (3.7) and (3.48) implies

∥𝐯∥Lp2→0​as​t→∞, 2<p2<p0.\lVert{\bf v}\rVert_{L^{p_{2}}}\to 0~~\text{as}~~t\to\infty,\ \ 2<{p_{2}}<p_{0}.

Hence (1.11) is proved and the proof of Theorem 1.1 is thus completed.

5. Proof of Theorem 1.2

In this section, we pass the results of the transformed chemotaxis model (1.5) to the original chemotaxis system (1). Noticing that the transformed and pre-transformed systems have the same quantity uu, we are left to prove the results for cc only. We start with the proof of (1.12). From the second equation of (1) and the Cole-Hopf transformation (1.4), we can derive that

(ln⁡c)t=−u(\ln c)_{t}=-u (5.1)

which together with c0>0c_{0}>0 and u≥0u\geq 0 gives

0≤c⁡(x,t)≤c⁡(x,0)=c0.0\leq c(x,t)\leq c(x,0)=c_{0}. (5.2)

Integrating (5.1) over [1,t)[1,t), we have from (5.2) that

c⁡(x,t)=c⁡(x,1)​exp⁡(−(t−1)−∫1t(u−1)​dτ)≤c0​exp⁡(−(t−1)−∫1t(u−1)​dτ).\begin{split}c(x,t)=&c(x,1)\exp\left(-(t-1)-\int_{1}^{t}(u-1)d\tau\right)\\ \leq&c_{0}\exp\left(-(t-1)-\int_{1}^{t}(u-1)d\tau\right).\end{split} (5.3)

From (3.37), we get

∫1t∥u−1∥L∞​dτ≤14​(t−1),\begin{split}\int_{1}^{t}\lVert u-1\rVert_{L^{\infty}}d\tau\leq\frac{1}{4}(t-1),\end{split}

which, along with (5.3) yields

∥c∥L∞≤C​e−34​(t−1)≤C​e−34​t.\begin{split}\lVert c\rVert_{L^{\infty}}\leq Ce^{-\frac{3}{4}(t-1)}\leq Ce^{-\frac{3}{4}t}.\end{split}

This completes the proof of Theorem 1.2.
